questions.exam_reasoning: Tests precise law-to-sector mapping across the core regulations.

source_reference.syllabus_section: Domain 1 > Security Governance and Compliance > Important Laws and Regulations

questions.question: A US-based e-commerce company stores and processes the personal data of customers living in Germany and France. Which regulation most directly governs how it must handle that customer data?

explanation.why_correct: Because the company processes personal data of EU residents, GDPR applies regardless of the company's US location.

why_others_are_wrong.A: HIPAA covers US health information, not general EU customer data.
why_others_are_wrong.B: SOX covers corporate financial disclosures, not customer personal data handling.
why_others_are_wrong.C: GLBA covers US financial-institution data privacy, not this scenario.

questions.exam_reasoning: Tests selecting the correct cross-border regulation by data-subject residency.

source_reference.syllabus_section: Domain 1 > Security Governance and Compliance > Determine Compliance Requirements

questions.question: A retailer that accepts branded credit cards must comply with security requirements for storing and transmitting cardholder data. Which framework applies?

explanation.why_correct: PCI DSS sets security standards for organizations that handle branded credit cards.

why_others_are_wrong.B: HIPAA covers health data.
why_others_are_wrong.D: GINA covers genetic information.
why_others_are_wrong.A: FISMA covers US federal agencies.

questions.exam_reasoning: Maps card-handling obligations to PCI DSS.

source_reference.syllabus_section: Domain 1 > Security Governance and Compliance > Important Laws and Regulations

questions.question: A company is contracting with vendors located in three different countries. From a compliance standpoint, the security professional should:

options.label: A
options.text: Consider the laws and regulations of each jurisdiction that applies to the engagement

options.label: B
options.text: Assume all countries share identical regulations

options.label: C
options.text: Defer entirely to whichever vendor has the lowest price

options.label: D
options.text: Apply only the laws of the company's home country and ignore the rest

explanation.why_correct: When contracting across countries, laws vary by jurisdiction, so each applicable legal framework must be understood and addressed.

why_others_are_wrong.D: Home-country law alone may not satisfy foreign jurisdictions' requirements.
why_others_are_wrong.B: Laws differ substantially between countries.
why_others_are_wrong.C: Price has no bearing on legal compliance obligations.

questions.exam_reasoning: Tests multi-jurisdiction compliance awareness.

source_reference.syllabus_section: Domain 1 > Security Governance and Compliance > Determine Compliance Requirements

questions.question: Which TWO regulations are most associated with the financial sector? (Select TWO.)

options.label: B
options.text: Health Insurance Portability and Accountability Act (HIPAA)

explanation.why_correct: GLBA governs financial-data privacy and SOX governs corporate financial disclosures—both financial-sector focused.

why_others_are_wrong.B: HIPAA is healthcare-focused.
why_others_are_wrong.C: GINA concerns genetic-information discrimination.

questions.exam_reasoning: Groups financial-sector regulations versus health/genetic ones.

source_reference.syllabus_section: Domain 1 > Security Governance and Compliance > Important Laws and Regulations

questions.question: A company protects its proprietary manufacturing process by keeping it secret and giving it competitive advantage, without registering it publicly. This protection is a:

explanation.why_correct: A trade secret protects secret methods or processes (recipes, designs, algorithms) that give a competitive advantage, relying on secrecy rather than public registration.

why_others_are_wrong.B: A patent requires public disclosure in exchange for time-limited exclusivity.
why_others_are_wrong.A: A trademark protects brand identifiers like names and logos.
why_others_are_wrong.C: A copyright protects original creative/literary works.

questions.exam_reasoning: Distinguishes secrecy-based protection (trade secret) from registered protections.

source_reference.syllabus_section: Domain 1 > Security Governance and Compliance > Licensing and Property Rights

questions.question: Which IP protection covers brand identifiers such as a unique product name, logo, or slogan?

explanation.why_correct: A trademark protects brand identifiers like names, logos, and slogans.

why_others_are_wrong.A: A patent protects inventions/designs.
why_others_are_wrong.D: A copyright protects creative/literary works.
why_others_are_wrong.C: A trade secret protects confidential competitive processes.

questions.exam_reasoning: Maps brand identifiers to trademarks.

source_reference.syllabus_section: Domain 1 > Security Governance and Compliance > Licensing and Property Rights

questions.question: Using someone else's copyrighted material generally requires:

options.label: A
options.text: Nothing, since copyright never restricts reuse

options.label: D
options.text: Permission or attribution as required by the license

explanation.why_correct: Use of copyrighted material requires permission or attribution per the applicable terms.

why_others_are_wrong.A: Copyright does restrict reuse without permission.
why_others_are_wrong.B: Patents protect inventions, not reuse of creative works.
why_others_are_wrong.C: Trademarks protect brand identifiers, unrelated to copyrighted-work reuse.

questions.exam_reasoning: Tests basic copyright reuse obligations.

source_reference.syllabus_section: Domain 1 > Security Governance and Compliance > Licensing and Property Rights

questions.question: An End User License Agreement (EULA) is best described as:

options.label: A
options.text: An internal company data classification label

options.label: B
options.text: A government statute regulating software exports

options.label: C
options.text: A binding agreement between the user and the license issuer governing product use

options.label: D
options.text: A free public-domain dedication of a work

explanation.why_correct: A EULA is a binding agreement between the user and the license issuer defining how the product may be used.

why_others_are_wrong.B: Export regulation is governed by EXIM controls, not a EULA.
why_others_are_wrong.D: Public-domain dedication is different from a EULA's binding terms.
why_others_are_wrong.A: Classification labels are internal asset-security artifacts.

questions.exam_reasoning: Recall of EULA as a binding use agreement.

source_reference.syllabus_section: Domain 1 > Security Governance and Compliance > Types of Licenses

questions.question: A license that grants lifetime authorization to use a product is a:

explanation.why_correct: A perpetual license grants lifetime authorization to use the product.

why_others_are_wrong.A: A subscription license is time-limited and renews.
why_others_are_wrong.D: Creative Commons is a free-use license for copyrighted materials.
why_others_are_wrong.B: A trade secret is an IP protection, not a license type.

questions.exam_reasoning: Recall of perpetual-license meaning.

source_reference.syllabus_section: Domain 1 > Security Governance and Compliance > Types of Licenses

questions.question: Creative Commons (CC) licenses are primarily used to:

options.label: A
options.text: Grant free use of copyrighted materials under defined conditions

options.label: B
options.text: Control the export of encryption technology

explanation.why_correct: Creative Commons provides free-use licensing for copyrighted materials under specified conditions.

why_others_are_wrong.D: Patents protect inventions, not free reuse of works.
why_others_are_wrong.C: Trademark registration protects brand identifiers.
why_others_are_wrong.B: Encryption export is an EXIM matter.

questions.exam_reasoning: Maps CC to free copyrighted-work licensing.

source_reference.syllabus_section: Domain 1 > Security Governance and Compliance > Types of Licenses

questions.question: Which TWO are recognized categories of intellectual property protection? (Select TWO.)

explanation.why_correct: Patents and copyrights are key intellectual property protections.

why_others_are_wrong.A: A baseline is a minimum set of security controls, not an IP protection.
why_others_are_wrong.C: A tactical plan is a mid-term security plan, not an IP protection.

questions.exam_reasoning: Separates genuine IP protections from unrelated governance terms.

source_reference.syllabus_section: Domain 1 > Security Governance and Compliance > Licensing and Property Rights

questions.question: A competitor secretly obtains a company's confidential product formulas by bribing an insider. This activity is BEST characterized as:

options.label: A
options.text: A protected exercise of fair use

options.label: D
options.text: Corporate espionage, which may constitute criminal activity beyond ethical competitive research

explanation.why_correct: Secretly acquiring protected information without the owner's permission is corporate espionage, going beyond ethical research and potentially criminal.

why_others_are_wrong.B: Legitimate competitive intelligence uses public/ethical sources, not bribery and theft.
why_others_are_wrong.C: No license grants access; this is unauthorized acquisition.
why_others_are_wrong.A: Fair use concerns limited copyrighted-work use, not theft of trade secrets.

questions.exam_reasoning: Distinguishes illegal espionage from legitimate competitive intelligence.

source_reference.syllabus_section: Domain 1 > Security Governance and Compliance > Corporate Espionage

questions.question: The World Intellectual Property Organization (WIPO) primarily:

options.label: A
options.text: Provides technical assistance for international intellectual property protection

explanation.why_correct: WIPO provides technical assistance for international IP protection.

why_others_are_wrong.C: Financial-disclosure rules are SOX (US).
why_others_are_wrong.D: Card standards are PCI DSS.
why_others_are_wrong.B: EU data-subject rights come from GDPR.

questions.exam_reasoning: Recall of WIPO's international IP role.

source_reference.syllabus_section: Domain 1 > Security Governance and Compliance > International Protection of Intellectual Property

questions.question: Export and Import Controls (EXIM) primarily aim to:

options.label: B
options.text: Prevent unauthorized access to trade secrets, controlled technologies, and sensitive data across borders

options.label: C
options.text: Define data-subject rights for EU residents

explanation.why_correct: EXIM controls regulate cross-border transfer of technology, goods, and services to prevent unauthorized access to controlled technologies and sensitive data.

why_others_are_wrong.D: Financial reporting is SOX, not EXIM.
why_others_are_wrong.C: EU data-subject rights are GDPR.
why_others_are_wrong.A: Password rules are technical/operational controls, not EXIM.

questions.exam_reasoning: Maps EXIM to cross-border technology/data control.

source_reference.syllabus_section: Domain 1 > Security Governance and Compliance > Export and Import Controls

questions.question: The Wassenaar Arrangement is most relevant to which security-related export concern?

options.label: A
options.text: Accuracy of public companies' financial statements

options.label: C
options.text: Privacy rights of EU data subjects

options.label: D
options.text: Controls on the export of items such as encryption technology across borders

explanation.why_correct: The Wassenaar Arrangement governs export controls, including categories covering encryption technology (e.g., Category 5).

why_others_are_wrong.C: EU privacy rights come from GDPR.
why_others_are_wrong.A: Financial-statement accuracy is SOX.
why_others_are_wrong.B: Health-information protection is HIPAA.

questions.exam_reasoning: Connects Wassenaar to encryption/technology export controls.

source_reference.syllabus_section: Domain 1 > Security Governance and Compliance > Export and Import Controls

questions.question: Mechanical components that could be used in both civilian products and military systems are an example of:

explanation.why_correct: Dual-use goods have both civilian and military applications and are therefore subject to special export controls.

why_others_are_wrong.B: Data localization concerns keeping data within a country's borders.
why_others_are_wrong.A: A perpetual license is a software-use term.
why_others_are_wrong.C: A PIA assesses privacy controls.

questions.exam_reasoning: Recognizes the dual-use concept in export control.

source_reference.syllabus_section: Domain 1 > Security Governance and Compliance > Export and Import Controls

questions.question: A country requires that its citizens' personal data be stored on servers physically located within its borders. This requirement is known as:

explanation.why_correct: Data localization mandates that certain data be stored (and sometimes processed) within a specific country's borders.

why_others_are_wrong.C: Transborder data flow refers to data crossing borders, the opposite emphasis.
why_others_are_wrong.A: Data portability is a GDPR right to reuse data across services.
why_others_are_wrong.B: Data classification is labeling data by sensitivity.

questions.exam_reasoning: Distinguishes data localization from transborder data flow.

source_reference.syllabus_section: Domain 1 > Security Governance and Compliance > Export and Import Controls

questions.question: A US company plans to ship its strong-encryption software to customers in several countries. To avoid violating export controls, it should FIRST:

options.label: A
options.text: Verify compliance with applicable export-control categories (e.g., Wassenaar Category 5) before shipping

options.label: B
options.text: Remove all encryption to avoid any controls, regardless of customer needs

options.label: C
options.text: Ship immediately and address any legal issues only if challenged

options.label: D
options.text: Assume software is exempt because it is intangible

explanation.why_correct: Encryption software exported without proper compliance can violate export-control categories (e.g., Wassenaar Category 5 Part 2), so compliance must be verified first.

why_others_are_wrong.C: Shipping first and reacting later risks legal violations and penalties.
why_others_are_wrong.B: Stripping needed functionality is not a compliance strategy and harms customers.
why_others_are_wrong.D: Software, including intangible delivery, is subject to export controls.

questions.exam_reasoning: Tests proactive export-control compliance for cryptographic software.

source_reference.syllabus_section: Domain 1 > Security Governance and Compliance > Export and Import Controls

questions.question: An attacker passively eavesdrops on network traffic to learn information without altering any system resources. This is a:

explanation.why_correct: A passive attack attempts to learn or use information from the system without affecting its resources.

why_others_are_wrong.D: An active attack alters system resources or affects operation.
why_others_are_wrong.B: A zero-day exploits a previously unknown vulnerability, not defined by passivity.
why_others_are_wrong.C: A destruction crime deliberately destroys data or systems.

questions.exam_reasoning: Distinguishes passive (observe) from active (alter) attacks.

source_reference.syllabus_section: Domain 1 > Security Governance and Compliance > Types of Cyber Attacks

questions.question: A zero-day attack occurs when attackers exploit:

options.label: B
options.text: A vulnerability that was patched years ago

options.label: C
options.text: A user who shares their password willingly

options.label: D
options.text: A previously unknown vulnerability that developers have not yet patched

explanation.why_correct: A zero-day exploits a previously unknown vulnerability that developers have not had time to address and patch.

why_others_are_wrong.B: An old patched vulnerability is not a zero-day.
why_others_are_wrong.A: A documented misconfiguration is a known issue, not a zero-day.
why_others_are_wrong.C: That describes social engineering, not a zero-day.

questions.exam_reasoning: Recall of the zero-day definition.

source_reference.syllabus_section: Domain 1 > Security Governance and Compliance > Types of Cyber Attacks

questions.question: A disgruntled systems administrator with legitimate network access copies confidential files to sell to a competitor. This threat actor is BEST classified as:

explanation.why_correct: An insider threat is an employee who has access to corporate networks and might exploit that access to steal information.

why_others_are_wrong.B: A script kiddie uses prebuilt tools and lacks sophisticated access/expertise; the key here is trusted insider access.
why_others_are_wrong.C: A state actor is government-sponsored; nothing indicates that.
why_others_are_wrong.A: A hacktivist is motivated by a cause; here the motive is personal/financial misuse of insider access.

questions.exam_reasoning: Tests recognizing insider misuse of legitimate access.

source_reference.syllabus_section: Domain 1 > Security Governance and Compliance > Types of Threat Actors

questions.question: An individual who uses existing scripts or tools to attack systems but lacks sophisticated expertise is a:

explanation.why_correct: A script kiddie uses existing scripts or code to hack, lacking sophisticated expertise.

why_others_are_wrong.A: A state actor is a sophisticated government-sponsored attacker.
why_others_are_wrong.C: An insider threat misuses legitimate access.
why_others_are_wrong.D: A data steward is an internal data-expertise role, not a threat actor.

questions.exam_reasoning: Recall of the script-kiddie definition.

source_reference.syllabus_section: Domain 1 > Security Governance and Compliance > Types of Threat Actors

questions.question: Which TWO are types of threat actors described in the guide? (Select TWO.)

explanation.why_correct: State actors (government-sponsored) and insider threats (trusted employees who misuse access) are both threat-actor types.

why_others_are_wrong.D: A baseline is a minimum set of controls, not a threat actor.
why_others_are_wrong.C: A tactical plan is a planning horizon, not a threat actor.

questions.exam_reasoning: Separates threat-actor types from governance terms.

source_reference.syllabus_section: Domain 1 > Security Governance and Compliance > Types of Threat Actors

questions.question: A highly resourced, government-sponsored group conducts a long-term espionage campaign against a defense contractor. This threat actor is BEST described as a:

explanation.why_correct: State actors are government-sponsored groups engaging in espionage and other cyber operations, typically well-resourced and persistent.

why_others_are_wrong.A: Script kiddies lack the sophistication and resources described.
why_others_are_wrong.D: A casual hacker would not mount a sustained, well-funded espionage campaign.
why_others_are_wrong.C: A disgruntled customer does not match a government-sponsored espionage profile.

questions.exam_reasoning: Tests recognizing the state-actor profile from resources and intent.

source_reference.syllabus_section: Domain 1 > Security Governance and Compliance > Types of Threat Actors

questions.question: An internal investigation conducted to determine whether an employee violated company policy, used to support an HR decision, is which type of investigation?

explanation.why_correct: Administrative investigations address internal policy violations and support internal/organizational decisions.

why_others_are_wrong.D: Criminal investigations involve potential violations of criminal law and law enforcement.
why_others_are_wrong.B: Civil investigations involve disputes between parties (e.g., contracts, damages).
why_others_are_wrong.C: Regulatory investigations involve compliance with a regulator's rules.

questions.exam_reasoning: Maps an internal policy-violation inquiry to the administrative type.

source_reference.syllabus_section: Domain 1 > Incident Management > Investigations (administrative, criminal, civil, regulatory)

questions.question: A case that could send a defendant to prison generally requires a higher standard of proof than a lawsuit seeking monetary damages. This contrast is BETWEEN which two investigation/case types?

options.label: A
options.text: Criminal (beyond a reasonable doubt) vs civil (preponderance of the evidence)

explanation.why_correct: Criminal cases require the highest standard (beyond a reasonable doubt), while civil cases use the lower preponderance-of-the-evidence standard.

why_others_are_wrong.D: "Awareness" is a training concept, not a case type.
why_others_are_wrong.C: "Perpetual" is a license type, not a case standard.
why_others_are_wrong.B: Creative Commons is a license, not an investigation type.

questions.exam_reasoning: Tests the differing standards of proof across criminal and civil matters.

source_reference.syllabus_section: Domain 1 > Incident Management > Investigations (administrative, criminal, civil, regulatory)

questions.question: An inquiry initiated by a government regulator to determine whether an organization complied with a specific industry rule is a(n):

explanation.why_correct: A regulatory investigation examines compliance with a regulator's rules or standards for an industry.

why_others_are_wrong.A: Administrative investigations are internal policy matters.
why_others_are_wrong.C: Criminal investigations pursue violations of criminal law.
why_others_are_wrong.D: Civil investigations concern disputes between private parties.

questions.exam_reasoning: Distinguishes regulatory from administrative, criminal, and civil investigations.

source_reference.syllabus_section: Domain 1 > Incident Management > Investigations (administrative, criminal, civil, regulatory)

questions.question: Which security document provides detailed, step-by-step instructions on how to implement a standard?

explanation.why_correct: A procedure provides detailed, step-by-step instructions on how to implement standards.

why_others_are_wrong.D: A policy is a high-level statement of management intent and goals.
why_others_are_wrong.C: A baseline defines the minimum security controls required to meet a standard.
why_others_are_wrong.B: A guideline offers recommendations/best practices when standards are unclear or non-specific.

questions.exam_reasoning: Distinguishes procedure (how-to steps) from policy, baseline, and guideline.

source_reference.syllabus_section: Domain 1 > Security Governance and Compliance > Security Compliance Artifacts

questions.question: The minimum set of security controls required to meet a standard, adjustable only through formal change management, is a:

explanation.why_correct: A baseline is the minimum security controls required to meet standards, changeable through formal change management.

why_others_are_wrong.C: A guideline is a non-mandatory recommendation.
why_others_are_wrong.A: A procedure is step-by-step implementation detail.
why_others_are_wrong.B: A policy is high-level management direction.

questions.exam_reasoning: Recall of baseline as the mandatory minimum control set.

source_reference.syllabus_section: Domain 1 > Security Governance and Compliance > Security Compliance Artifacts

questions.question: Which document type is a recommendation or best practice used when standards or procedures are unclear or non-specific, and is generally NOT mandatory?

explanation.why_correct: A guideline provides recommendations/best practices when standards or procedures are unclear or non-specific, and is advisory rather than mandatory.

why_others_are_wrong.A: A standard is a mandatory, specific requirement.
why_others_are_wrong.C: A baseline is a mandatory minimum control set.
why_others_are_wrong.D: A procedure is mandatory step-by-step instruction.

questions.exam_reasoning: Identifies the guideline as the advisory document.

source_reference.syllabus_section: Domain 1 > Security Governance and Compliance > Security Compliance Artifacts

questions.question: A document that sets specific, mandatory requirements aligning with organizational policy (for example, requiring AES-256 for data at rest) is a:

explanation.why_correct: A standard sets specific mandatory requirements that align with and detail how to comply with policy.

why_others_are_wrong.A: A guideline is advisory, not mandatory.
why_others_are_wrong.B: A policy is higher-level intent, not the specific requirement.
why_others_are_wrong.D: A baseline is the minimum control set; the specific mandatory requirement is the standard.

questions.exam_reasoning: Distinguishes a standard's specific mandate from policy and guideline.

source_reference.syllabus_section: Domain 1 > Security Governance and Compliance > Security Compliance Artifacts

questions.question: A policy that defines the organization's overall security goals and responsibilities at the highest level is a(n):

explanation.why_correct: An organizational (program) policy defines organization-wide security goals and responsibilities.

why_others_are_wrong.B: An issue-specific policy addresses a particular topic (e.g., email use).
why_others_are_wrong.C: A system-specific policy applies to a particular system.
why_others_are_wrong.A: A procedure is implementation detail, not a policy tier.

questions.exam_reasoning: Distinguishes organizational, issue-specific, and system-specific policies.

source_reference.syllabus_section: Domain 1 > Security Governance and Compliance > Types of Policies

questions.question: Which TWO statements about security documentation are correct? (Select TWO.)

options.label: A
options.text: Standards are mandatory and detail specific requirements that support policy

options.label: B
options.text: Baselines are optional suggestions that require no change control

options.label: C
options.text: Guidelines are advisory recommendations used when standards are unclear

options.label: D
options.text: Policies are step-by-step technical instructions for administrators

explanation.why_correct: Standards are mandatory and specific; guidelines are advisory best practices—both stated correctly.

why_others_are_wrong.D: Policies are high-level intent; procedures (not policies) are step-by-step instructions.
why_others_are_wrong.B: Baselines are mandatory minimums adjusted only through formal change management, not optional.

questions.exam_reasoning: Tests correct relationships among policy, standard, baseline, procedure, and guideline.

source_reference.syllabus_section: Domain 1 > Security Governance and Compliance > Security Compliance Artifacts

questions.question: According to the guide, risk arises from the combination of:

explanation.why_correct: Threats and vulnerabilities together create risk; risk management identifies, assesses, and mitigates that risk.

why_others_are_wrong.A: Policies and procedures are governance documents, not the components of risk.
why_others_are_wrong.B: Awareness and training are controls that reduce risk, not its definition.
why_others_are_wrong.D: Patents and trademarks are IP protections, unrelated to the risk formula.

questions.exam_reasoning: Confirms the threat-plus-vulnerability basis of risk.

source_reference.syllabus_section: Domain 1 > Risk Management > Risk Management Concepts

questions.question: A company purchases cyber-insurance so that a third party bears much of the financial loss from a potential breach. Which risk response is this?

explanation.why_correct: Transferring the responsibility/accountability of a risk to another party (e.g., via insurance) is risk assignment (transfer).

why_others_are_wrong.A: Avoidance means not undertaking the risky activity at all.
why_others_are_wrong.B: Acceptance means acknowledging and bearing the residual risk.
why_others_are_wrong.D: Deterrence implements controls to discourage the threat, not shift the loss.

questions.exam_reasoning: Maps insurance to risk transfer/assignment.

source_reference.syllabus_section: Domain 1 > Risk Management > Risk Response and Monitoring

questions.question: After assessing the risk, a company decides NOT to launch a new product line that would expose it to unacceptable regulatory risk. Which risk response is this?

explanation.why_correct: Choosing not to engage in an activity that introduces higher risk is risk avoidance.

why_others_are_wrong.A: Acceptance would mean proceeding and bearing the residual risk.
why_others_are_wrong.C: Mitigation would mean proceeding but reducing the risk with controls.
why_others_are_wrong.B: Assignment would mean transferring the risk to another party.

questions.exam_reasoning: Maps declining the risky activity to avoidance.

source_reference.syllabus_section: Domain 1 > Risk Management > Risk Response and Monitoring

questions.question: After applying controls, management formally acknowledges and decides to live with the remaining risk. The remaining risk and the decision are, respectively:

explanation.why_correct: The risk left after responses are applied is residual risk; choosing to live with it is risk acceptance.

why_others_are_wrong.A: Inherent risk is the risk before controls; avoidance is declining the activity.
why_others_are_wrong.D: Total risk is before controls; assignment transfers risk to another party.
why_others_are_wrong.C: A threat is a potential cause of harm; deterrence discourages it.

questions.exam_reasoning: Tests the residual-risk concept and its acceptance.

source_reference.syllabus_section: Domain 1 > Risk Management > Risk Response and Monitoring

questions.question: Implementing controls to reduce a risk to an acceptable level is known as:

explanation.why_correct: Risk mitigation reduces risk to an acceptable level through various controls.

why_others_are_wrong.B: Acceptance bears the risk without reducing it.
why_others_are_wrong.C: Avoidance declines the risky activity entirely.
why_others_are_wrong.A: Transfer shifts the risk to another party.

questions.exam_reasoning: Recall of mitigation as risk reduction via controls.

source_reference.syllabus_section: Domain 1 > Risk Management > Risk Response and Monitoring

questions.question: Which TWO of the following are recognized risk response strategies in the guide? (Select TWO.)

explanation.why_correct: Risk deterrence (deterrent controls to reduce likelihood/impact) and risk acceptance (bearing residual risk) are recognized responses.

why_others_are_wrong.A: "Risk amplification" is not a recognized response—organizations seek to reduce, not amplify, risk.
why_others_are_wrong.B: "Risk capitalization" is not a defined risk response strategy.

questions.exam_reasoning: Separates genuine risk responses from invented terms.

source_reference.syllabus_section: Domain 1 > Risk Management > Risk Response and Monitoring

questions.question: A security awareness policy that employees must follow is which CATEGORY of control?

explanation.why_correct: Administrative controls are procedures and processes (soft/process controls), such as policies and training.

why_others_are_wrong.B: Technical/logical controls protect assets through hardware/software mechanisms.
why_others_are_wrong.A: Physical controls protect tangible assets and facilities.
why_others_are_wrong.C: "Recovery" is a control TYPE (function), not one of the three categories.

questions.exam_reasoning: Distinguishes control categories (admin/technical/physical) from control types.

source_reference.syllabus_section: Domain 1 > Risk Management > Controls and Countermeasures

questions.question: A locked door with a "Authorized Personnel Only" sign that discourages intruders before any attempt is primarily which TYPE of control?

explanation.why_correct: Deterrent controls discourage unauthorized actions before they occur; signage that dissuades intrusion is deterrent.

why_others_are_wrong.B: Corrective controls modify the environment to fix issues after an event.
why_others_are_wrong.C: Recovery controls restore operations after an event.
why_others_are_wrong.A: Compensating controls substitute for a primary control that is infeasible.

questions.exam_reasoning: Tests classifying a control by its function (deter before the act).

source_reference.syllabus_section: Domain 1 > Risk Management > Types of Controls

questions.question: An organization cannot apply the required encryption on a legacy system, so it isolates that system on a restricted network segment to provide equivalent protection. The network isolation is BEST classified as which type of control?

explanation.why_correct: A compensating control provides an alternative that supports or substitutes for a primary control that cannot be implemented.

why_others_are_wrong.A: Detective controls discover events after they occur; isolation is preventive/compensating here.
why_others_are_wrong.C: Deterrent controls discourage actions psychologically; isolation actively restricts access.
why_others_are_wrong.B: Directive controls direct behavior via policy; this is a technical substitute control.

questions.exam_reasoning: Tests recognizing a compensating control when the primary control is infeasible.

source_reference.syllabus_section: Domain 1 > Risk Management > Types of Controls

questions.question: Combining administrative, technical, and physical controls in multiple layers so that no single failure exposes the asset is the strategy known as:

explanation.why_correct: Defense in depth layers multiple, varied controls so the failure of one does not compromise the whole.

why_others_are_wrong.D: Single sign-on is an authentication convenience, not a layered-defense strategy.
why_others_are_wrong.B: Risk acceptance is a risk response, not a control architecture.
why_others_are_wrong.C: Data localization concerns where data is stored geographically.

questions.exam_reasoning: Recall of defense in depth as layered, varied controls.

source_reference.syllabus_section: Domain 1 > Risk Management > Controls and Countermeasures

questions.question: A proposed safeguard costs $50,000 per year to protect an asset whose total value is $20,000. According to the cost-benefit principle, the organization should:

options.label: A
options.text: Reconsider, because a control should not cost more than the value of the asset it protects

options.label: B
options.text: Implement it immediately, since more security is always better

options.label: C
options.text: Transfer the asset's ownership to avoid the decision

options.label: D
options.text: Implement it because all assets must have maximum protection

explanation.why_correct: The cost-benefit principle states a control's cost should not exceed the asset value or the benefit gained; spending $50k to protect a $20k asset is not justified.

why_others_are_wrong.B: "More is always better" ignores cost-benefit and wastes resources.
why_others_are_wrong.D: Maximum protection regardless of value contradicts the cost-benefit principle.
why_others_are_wrong.C: Transferring ownership does not address the disproportionate safeguard cost.

questions.exam_reasoning: Applies the safeguard cost-vs-asset-value principle.

source_reference.syllabus_section: Domain 1 > Risk Management > Controls and Countermeasures

questions.question: Which TWO are categories (not types) of security controls? (Select TWO.)

explanation.why_correct: Technical/logical and physical are control CATEGORIES (alongside administrative). Detective and corrective are control TYPES/functions.

why_others_are_wrong.D: Detective is a control type/function, not a category.
why_others_are_wrong.C: Corrective is a control type/function, not a category.

questions.exam_reasoning: Reinforces the category-vs-type distinction.

source_reference.syllabus_section: Domain 1 > Risk Management > Controls and Countermeasures

questions.question: Which framework is identified as the primary CISSP-exam reference for Information Security Continuous Monitoring (ISCM)?

explanation.why_correct: NIST SP 800-137 (ISCM) is highlighted as the primary continuous-monitoring reference for the exam.

why_others_are_wrong.B: ISO 28000 is a supply-chain security management standard.
why_others_are_wrong.C: PCI DSS is a payment-card security standard.
why_others_are_wrong.A: NIST SP 800-30 covers risk assessment, not continuous monitoring specifically.

questions.exam_reasoning: Maps ISCM to NIST SP 800-137.

source_reference.syllabus_section: Domain 1 > Risk Management > Continuous Monitoring

questions.question: How does continuous monitoring (continuous improvement) differ from simple system monitoring?

options.label: A
options.text: It evaluates the effectiveness of all types of security controls, not just log/system status review

options.label: B
options.text: It replaces the need for any security controls

options.label: C
options.text: It only runs once during system authorization

options.label: D
options.text: It is limited strictly to reviewing firewall logs

explanation.why_correct: Continuous monitoring focuses on evaluating security control implementations and effectiveness across all control types—broader than log-file or system-status review.

why_others_are_wrong.D: It is not restricted to firewall logs or log review.
why_others_are_wrong.C: It is ongoing, not a one-time authorization activity.
why_others_are_wrong.B: It assesses controls; it does not replace them.

questions.exam_reasoning: Tests that continuous monitoring evaluates control effectiveness broadly.

source_reference.syllabus_section: Domain 1 > Risk Management > Continuous Monitoring

questions.question: Place the following NIST Risk Management Framework (RMF) steps in their correct order, beginning after the Prepare step. (Provide the option labels in order.)

explanation.why_correct: Following Prepare, the RMF proceeds: Categorize the system, Select controls, Implement them, Assess effectiveness, Authorize operation based on residual risk, then Monitor continuously.

questions.exam_reasoning: Tests the ordered RMF lifecycle (NIST SP 800-37).

source_reference.syllabus_section: Domain 1 > Risk Management > Risk Frameworks

questions.question: Which set correctly lists the five core functions of the NIST Cybersecurity Framework (CSF)?

explanation.why_correct: The NIST CSF core functions are Identify, Protect, Detect, Respond, and Recover.

why_others_are_wrong.B: Plan-Do-Check-Act is the Deming cycle, not the CSF core.
why_others_are_wrong.C: Those are RMF steps, not CSF functions.
why_others_are_wrong.A: Those are risk-response strategies, not CSF functions.

questions.exam_reasoning: Recall of the five CSF core functions.

source_reference.syllabus_section: Domain 1 > Risk Management > NIST Cybersecurity Framework

questions.question: Which framework is an enterprise risk management framework used primarily for corporate governance and compliance with Sarbanes-Oxley?

explanation.why_correct: COSO is an enterprise risk management framework used primarily for corporate governance and SOX compliance.

why_others_are_wrong.D: ISO 31000 is a general, industry-agnostic risk management framework.
why_others_are_wrong.A: NIST SP 800-137 covers continuous monitoring.
why_others_are_wrong.B: SABSA is a business-driven security architecture framework.

questions.exam_reasoning: Distinguishes COSO (governance/SOX) from general and architecture frameworks.

source_reference.syllabus_section: Domain 1 > Risk Management > Risk Frameworks

questions.question: SABSA is best described as a framework for:

options.label: A
options.text: Protecting payment card data in retail environments

options.label: B
options.text: Governing the export of dual-use technologies

options.label: D
options.text: Developing business-driven, risk-focused security architectures aligned to business objectives

explanation.why_correct: SABSA provides a structured approach to business-driven, risk-focused security architecture that traces decisions back to business requirements.

why_others_are_wrong.A: Payment-card protection is PCI DSS.
why_others_are_wrong.B: Dual-use export is governed by EXIM/Wassenaar.
why_others_are_wrong.C: EU privacy rights come from GDPR.

questions.exam_reasoning: Identifies SABSA as a business-aligned security architecture framework.

source_reference.syllabus_section: Domain 1 > Risk Management > Understanding SABSA

questions.question: ISO/IEC 27001 is primarily a standard for:

options.label: A
options.text: Securing the physical supply chain of goods

options.label: B
options.text: Rating the severity of software vulnerabilities

options.label: C
options.text: Establishing and managing an information security management system (ISMS) to manage information security risk

explanation.why_correct: ISO/IEC 27001 defines requirements for an ISMS to manage information security risks and ensure compliance, grounded in the CIA triad.

why_others_are_wrong.A: Supply-chain security management is ISO 28000.
why_others_are_wrong.B: Vulnerability severity rating is associated with CVSS, not ISO 27001.
why_others_are_wrong.D: Encryption export is an EXIM/Wassenaar matter.

questions.exam_reasoning: Maps ISO 27001 to ISMS-based risk management.

source_reference.syllabus_section: Domain 1 > Risk Management > ISO/IEC 27001

questions.question: An asset is valued at $200,000. A particular fire scenario is expected to destroy 25% of the asset. What is the Single Loss Expectancy (SLE)?

explanation.why_correct: SLE = Asset Value × Exposure Factor = $200,000 × 0.25 = $50,000.

why_others_are_wrong.C: $25,000 would result from a 12.5% EF, not 25%.
why_others_are_wrong.D: $200,000 is the full asset value (100% EF), not 25%.
why_others_are_wrong.A: $800,000 incorrectly multiplies rather than applies the 25% exposure factor.

questions.exam_reasoning: Tests the SLE = AV × EF calculation.

source_reference.syllabus_section: Domain 1 > Risk Assessment > Conducting Risk Assessments

questions.question: A single loss event costs $50,000 (SLE) and is expected to occur twice per year (ARO = 2). What is the Annualized Loss Expectancy (ALE)?

why_others_are_wrong.C: $50,000 is the SLE for a single occurrence, not annualized.
why_others_are_wrong.A: $25,000 would halve rather than double the SLE.
why_others_are_wrong.D: $2,000 confuses the ARO value with a dollar amount.

questions.exam_reasoning: Tests the ALE = SLE × ARO calculation.

source_reference.syllabus_section: Domain 1 > Risk Assessment > Conducting Risk Assessments

questions.question: The Exposure Factor (EF) represents:

options.label: A
options.text: The total monetary cost of acquiring the asset

options.label: B
options.text: The annual cost of a safeguard

options.label: C
options.text: The number of times per year a risk occurs

options.label: D
options.text: The percentage of an asset's value likely to be lost if a risk is realized

explanation.why_correct: The EF is the percentage of asset value that could be lost when a risk is realized.

why_others_are_wrong.C: That describes the Annualized Rate of Occurrence (ARO).
why_others_are_wrong.A: That describes the Asset Value (AV).
why_others_are_wrong.B: That describes the annual cost of a safeguard.

questions.exam_reasoning: Recall of EF as a percentage of loss.

source_reference.syllabus_section: Domain 1 > Risk Assessment > Conducting Risk Assessments

questions.question: The Annualized Rate of Occurrence (ARO) is:

options.label: A
options.text: The estimated frequency at which a specific risk is expected to occur within a year

options.label: B
options.text: The expected loss from a single event

options.label: C
options.text: The percentage of asset value lost per event

options.label: D
options.text: The total value of the asset

explanation.why_correct: ARO is the estimated number of times a specific risk is expected to occur within a year.

why_others_are_wrong.C: That is the Exposure Factor (EF).
why_others_are_wrong.D: That is the Asset Value (AV).
why_others_are_wrong.B: That is the Single Loss Expectancy (SLE).

questions.exam_reasoning: Recall of ARO as annual frequency.

source_reference.syllabus_section: Domain 1 > Risk Assessment > Conducting Risk Assessments

questions.question: A server worth $40,000 faces a threat with a 50% exposure factor that is expected to occur 3 times per year. What is the ALE?

why_others_are_wrong.A: $20,000 is the SLE, not the annualized figure.
why_others_are_wrong.B: $120,000 applies the full asset value (100% EF) instead of 50%.
why_others_are_wrong.C: $6,000 misplaces a decimal in the calculation.

questions.exam_reasoning: Tests chaining SLE = AV × EF then ALE = SLE × ARO.

source_reference.syllabus_section: Domain 1 > Risk Assessment > Conducting Risk Assessments

questions.question: Which statement BEST distinguishes quantitative from qualitative risk assessment?

options.label: A
options.text: They produce identical outputs and are interchangeable

options.label: B
options.text: Quantitative is always faster and requires no data

options.label: C
options.text: Quantitative uses numerical/monetary values; qualitative uses subjective rankings such as high/medium/low

options.label: D
options.text: Quantitative uses color codes; qualitative uses precise dollar figures

explanation.why_correct: Quantitative assessment uses numerical/monetary values (AV, SLE, ALE), while qualitative uses subjective judgment and categories like high/low/moderate.

why_others_are_wrong.D: Reversed: color codes/categories are qualitative; dollar figures are quantitative.
why_others_are_wrong.B: Quantitative analysis requires substantial data and is not effort-free.
why_others_are_wrong.A: They differ in method and output and are not interchangeable.

questions.exam_reasoning: Tests the core difference between the two assessment approaches.

source_reference.syllabus_section: Domain 1 > Risk Assessment > Conducting Risk Assessments

questions.question: Which TWO equations are correct as defined in the guide? (Select TWO.)

options.label: B
options.text: ALE = SLE × Annualized Rate of Occurrence

options.label: C
options.text: SLE = ALE × Annualized Rate of Occurrence

explanation.why_correct: SLE = AV × EF and ALE = SLE × ARO are the correct definitions.

why_others_are_wrong.D: AV × EF yields SLE, not ALE.
why_others_are_wrong.C: This inverts the relationship; ALE is derived from SLE, not vice versa.

questions.exam_reasoning: Tests precise knowledge of the SLE and ALE formulas.

source_reference.syllabus_section: Domain 1 > Risk Assessment > Conducting Risk Assessments

questions.question: The Delphi technique supports qualitative risk assessment by:

options.label: A
options.text: Gathering anonymous expert consensus to reduce bias and undue influence

explanation.why_correct: The Delphi technique gathers consensus among experts through anonymous feedback, helping make unbiased decisions.

why_others_are_wrong.D: Exact monetary figures are the realm of quantitative assessment.
why_others_are_wrong.B: Vulnerability scanning is a technical assessment activity, not Delphi.
why_others_are_wrong.C: Encryption is a control, not a consensus technique.

questions.exam_reasoning: Maps anonymous expert consensus to the Delphi technique.

source_reference.syllabus_section: Domain 1 > Risk Assessment > Conducting Risk Assessments

questions.question: The level of risk an organization is willing to accept is referred to as its:

explanation.why_correct: Risk tolerance/risk appetite is the level of risk an organization is willing to accept.

why_others_are_wrong.C: Exposure factor is the percentage of asset value lost in an event.
why_others_are_wrong.D: "Residual control" is not a defined term; residual risk is what remains after controls.
why_others_are_wrong.B: ALE is a calculated annual loss figure, not a willingness threshold.

questions.exam_reasoning: Recall of the risk tolerance/appetite concept.

source_reference.syllabus_section: Domain 1 > Risk Assessment > Understanding Risk Assessments

questions.question: Under NIST SP 800-30, after conducting the assessment a team must communicate findings to senior management. The guidance emphasizes that this reporting should be:

options.label: A
options.text: Limited to a single numerical score with no context

options.label: B
options.text: Withheld from management to avoid alarm

options.label: C
options.text: Expressed in understandable business language to aid management decision-making

options.label: D
options.text: Written only in deep technical jargon for engineers

explanation.why_correct: NIST SP 800-30 reporting communicates findings to senior management in understandable business language to aid decision-making.

why_others_are_wrong.D: Technical jargon impairs management decision-making.
why_others_are_wrong.B: Withholding findings defeats the purpose of the assessment.
why_others_are_wrong.A: A bare score without context does not support informed decisions.

questions.exam_reasoning: Tests audience-appropriate risk reporting to leadership.

source_reference.syllabus_section: Domain 1 > Risk Assessment > NIST Special Publication 800-30 Risk Assessment Steps

questions.question: In the STRIDE threat-modeling methodology, the "R" represents which threat category?

explanation.why_correct: STRIDE stands for Spoofing, Tampering, Repudiation, Information disclosure, Denial of service, and Elevation of privilege; "R" is Repudiation.

why_others_are_wrong.D: Reconnaissance is an attack phase, not a STRIDE element.
why_others_are_wrong.B: Recovery is a control function, not a STRIDE element.
why_others_are_wrong.A: Redundancy is an availability technique, not a STRIDE element.

questions.exam_reasoning: Tests knowledge of the STRIDE categories.

source_reference.syllabus_section: Domain 1 > Risk Assessment > Threat Modeling Methodologies

questions.question: Which of the following is a recognized threat-modeling methodology referenced in the guide?

explanation.why_correct: PASTA (Process for Attack Simulation and Threat Analysis) is a recognized threat-modeling methodology, alongside STRIDE and DREAD.

why_others_are_wrong.A: PIPEDA is a Canadian privacy law.
why_others_are_wrong.C: PCI DSS is a payment-card security standard.
why_others_are_wrong.B: PERT is a project-scheduling technique, not threat modeling.

questions.exam_reasoning: Identifies PASTA as a threat-modeling methodology among distractors.

source_reference.syllabus_section: Domain 1 > Risk Assessment > Threat Modeling Methodologies

questions.question: In threat modeling, the sum of all points where an attacker could attempt to enter or extract data from a system is the:

explanation.why_correct: The attack surface is the total set of points (interfaces, inputs) through which an attacker could interact with or compromise a system.

why_others_are_wrong.A: Exposure factor is a percentage of loss in quantitative risk.
why_others_are_wrong.D: Residual risk is the risk remaining after controls.
why_others_are_wrong.C: A baseline is a minimum control set.

questions.exam_reasoning: Recall of the attack-surface concept.

source_reference.syllabus_section: Domain 1 > Risk Assessment > Threat Modeling Concepts

questions.question: A development team performs threat modeling during the DESIGN phase of a new application, before any code is written, to anticipate attacks. This approach is BEST described as:

explanation.why_correct: Anticipating threats early (e.g., at design, before exploitation) is a proactive approach to threat modeling.

why_others_are_wrong.D: A reactive approach responds after threats or incidents have manifested.
why_others_are_wrong.A: Penetration testing actively tests a running system, not design-phase modeling.
why_others_are_wrong.B: Incident response handles events after they occur.

questions.exam_reasoning: Distinguishes proactive (design-time) from reactive threat modeling.

source_reference.syllabus_section: Domain 1 > Risk Assessment > Threat Modeling Concepts

questions.question: Supply Chain Risk Management (SCRM) primarily addresses risks arising from:

options.label: A
options.text: An organization's dependence on external vendors and suppliers for goods and services

options.label: C
options.text: The classification level of internal documents

options.label: D
options.text: The accuracy of corporate financial statements

explanation.why_correct: SCRM addresses security risks in the supply chain due to dependencies on external sources for operational components, goods, and services.

why_others_are_wrong.B: Travel safety is a personnel-security topic, not SCRM.
why_others_are_wrong.D: Financial-statement accuracy is a SOX/governance concern.
why_others_are_wrong.C: Document classification is an asset-security activity.

questions.exam_reasoning: Maps SCRM to third-party/vendor dependency risk.

source_reference.syllabus_section: Domain 1 > Risk Management > Supply Chain Risk Management

questions.question: Which TWO are recognized categories of supply-chain risk described in the guide? (Select TWO.)

options.label: A
options.text: Awareness risks such as fewer posters in the lobby

options.label: B
options.text: Software risks such as vulnerabilities or malicious code

options.label: C
options.text: Risk appetite risks such as choosing the wrong color code

options.label: D
options.text: Hardware risks such as counterfeit components

explanation.why_correct: The guide lists hardware risks (counterfeits, embedded spyware), software risks (vulnerabilities, malcode, licensing), and service risks as supply-chain risk categories.

why_others_are_wrong.C: "Risk appetite color codes" relate to qualitative assessment, not a supply-chain risk category.
why_others_are_wrong.A: Poster counts relate to awareness delivery, not supply-chain risk.

questions.exam_reasoning: Identifies genuine supply-chain risk categories.

source_reference.syllabus_section: Domain 1 > Risk Management > Supply Chain Risk Management

questions.question: An organization wants to hold a critical cloud supplier contractually accountable for specific security requirements and define how compliance will be verified. The MOST appropriate mechanism is to:

options.label: A
options.text: Assume the vendor's marketing claims are sufficient assurance

options.label: B
options.text: Rely on a verbal understanding with the vendor's sales representative

options.label: C
options.text: Avoid documenting requirements to remain flexible

options.label: D
options.text: Establish a Service Level Agreement (SLA) that defines the security requirements and verification

explanation.why_correct: SLAs with suppliers define specific security requirements and acquisition policies, and support assessment of compliance.

why_others_are_wrong.B: Verbal understandings are unenforceable and unverifiable.
why_others_are_wrong.A: Marketing claims are not contractual assurance.
why_others_are_wrong.C: Failing to document requirements undermines accountability and verification.

questions.exam_reasoning: Tests using SLAs to enforce and verify supplier security obligations.

source_reference.syllabus_section: Domain 1 > Risk Management > Supply Chain Risk Management

questions.question: Objective 1.7 focuses on identifying, analyzing, assessing, prioritizing, and implementing requirements for:

explanation.why_correct: Objective 1.7 concerns identifying, analyzing, assessing, prioritizing, and implementing Business Continuity (BC) requirements.

why_others_are_wrong.D: Software licensing is part of legal/IP topics.
why_others_are_wrong.B: Key generation is a cryptography topic.
why_others_are_wrong.A: Marketing campaigns are unrelated to continuity planning.

questions.exam_reasoning: Anchors objective 1.7 to Business Continuity requirements.

source_reference.syllabus_section: Domain 1 > Business Continuity and Disaster Recovery > Business Continuity (BC) requirements

questions.question: When implementing Business Continuity requirements, an organization must decide which processes to restore first after a disruption. This prioritization should be driven primarily by:

options.label: A
options.text: The alphabetical order of system names

options.label: C
options.text: The relative criticality and impact of each business process on the organization

options.label: D
options.text: The personal preference of the newest employee

explanation.why_correct: BC requirements are prioritized by analyzing and assessing the criticality and impact of business processes, so the most critical are restored first.

why_others_are_wrong.B: Loudness of complaints is not an objective impact-based criterion.
why_others_are_wrong.A: Alphabetical ordering ignores business criticality.
why_others_are_wrong.D: Personal preference is not a valid prioritization basis.

questions.exam_reasoning: Tests impact/criticality-driven prioritization in continuity planning.

source_reference.syllabus_section: Domain 1 > Business Continuity and Disaster Recovery > Business Continuity (BC) requirements

questions.question: What is the PRIMARY purpose of classifying information and assets?

options.label: A
options.text: To make all data publicly accessible by default

options.label: B
options.text: To increase the total number of assets an organization owns

options.label: C
options.text: To determine how data should be handled and secured based on its criticality, sensitivity, and value

options.label: D
options.text: To eliminate the need for any security controls

explanation.why_correct: Classification identifies and ranks information/assets by criticality, sensitivity, and value so the right handling and protection are applied.

why_others_are_wrong.B: Classification organizes and protects existing assets; it does not increase asset count.
why_others_are_wrong.D: Classification drives appropriate controls; it does not remove the need for them.
why_others_are_wrong.A: Classification restricts sensitive data; it does not make everything public.

questions.exam_reasoning: Tests the core reason for classification: aligning protection to data value/sensitivity.

source_reference.syllabus_section: Domain 2 > Asset Security > Classifying Data and Assets

questions.question: When assigning a classification level, an organization should evaluate data primarily on the basis of its:

options.label: B
options.text: Number of employees who created it

options.label: C
options.text: Criticality, sensitivity, and value to the organization

explanation.why_correct: Data is classified based on its criticality, sensitivity, and value to the organization, which determine the required protection.

why_others_are_wrong.A: File size/format does not determine sensitivity or required protection.
why_others_are_wrong.D: Hardware age is an asset-lifecycle concern, not a classification criterion.
why_others_are_wrong.B: The number of creators is irrelevant to data sensitivity.

questions.exam_reasoning: Reinforces the criteria that drive classification decisions.

source_reference.syllabus_section: Domain 2 > Asset Security > Classifying Data and Assets

questions.question: In the government classification scheme described in the guide, which level applies to information whose disclosure would cause EXTREMELY high impact and the most significant damage?

explanation.why_correct: Top Secret denotes extremely high impact on disclosure with significant damage potential—the highest level.

why_others_are_wrong.A: Secret causes serious (high) damage, but less than Top Secret.
why_others_are_wrong.D: Confidential causes moderate/noticeable damage.
why_others_are_wrong.B: Unclassified has low or no impact.

questions.exam_reasoning: Tests ordering of government classification levels by impact.

source_reference.syllabus_section: Domain 2 > Asset Security > Classification Levels

questions.question: Which government classification level corresponds to information that would cause MODERATE impact (noticeable damage) if disclosed?

explanation.why_correct: Confidential corresponds to moderate impact—noticeable damage if disclosed.

why_others_are_wrong.A: Top Secret is extremely high impact.
why_others_are_wrong.B: Secret is high impact with serious damage.
why_others_are_wrong.D: Unclassified is low or no impact.

questions.exam_reasoning: Distinguishes Confidential (moderate) from higher and lower levels.

source_reference.syllabus_section: Domain 2 > Asset Security > Classification Levels

questions.question: Match each government classification level (1-4) to the impact of its disclosure (A-D).

options.label: A
options.text: Extremely high impact; significant damage potential

options.label: B
options.text: Low or no impact; minimal value information

options.label: D
options.text: High impact; serious damage if disclosed

explanation.why_correct: Top Secret → extremely high impact (B); Secret → high/serious damage (C); Confidential → moderate/noticeable (D); Unclassified → low/no impact (A).

questions.exam_reasoning: Tests precise mapping of classification levels to disclosure impact.

source_reference.syllabus_section: Domain 2 > Asset Security > Classification Levels

questions.question: A private retail company wants a classification scheme that fits its business rather than military labels. Which set of levels is MOST appropriate for a commercial organization?

options.label: A
options.text: No classification, since commercial data is never sensitive

options.label: C
options.text: Public, Internal, Sensitive (commercial tiers aligned to business needs)

options.label: D
options.text: Tier 0, Tier 1, Tier 2 hardware tiers used for data sensitivity

explanation.why_correct: Commercial organizations typically use business-aligned levels such as public, internal, and sensitive; classification should align with business needs.

why_others_are_wrong.B: Top Secret/Secret/Confidential are government/military labels, not the natural commercial fit.
why_others_are_wrong.D: Tier 0/1/2 are asset (system) tiers, not data sensitivity labels.
why_others_are_wrong.A: Commercial data (e.g., PII, proprietary data) is frequently sensitive and must be classified.

questions.exam_reasoning: Tests choosing business-aligned commercial classification over military labels.

source_reference.syllabus_section: Domain 2 > Asset Security > Classifying Data and Assets

questions.question: Using the asset classification tiers in the guide, critical servers, databases, and network devices belong to which tier?

explanation.why_correct: Tier 0 (Essential) covers critical servers, databases, and network devices.

why_others_are_wrong.B: Tier 1 (Important) covers development environments and backup systems.
why_others_are_wrong.A: Tier 2 (Non-Essential) covers workstations, mobile devices, and printers.
why_others_are_wrong.C: "Tier 3 (Disposable)" is not a tier defined in the guide.

questions.exam_reasoning: Tests recall of the most critical asset tier.

source_reference.syllabus_section: Domain 2 > Asset Security > Asset Classification Tiers

questions.question: Workstations, mobile devices, and printers are categorized in which asset tier?

explanation.why_correct: Tier 2 (Non-Essential) includes workstations, mobile devices, and printers.

why_others_are_wrong.C: Tier 0 is essential infrastructure such as critical servers and databases.
why_others_are_wrong.A: Tier 1 is important systems like development environments and backups.
why_others_are_wrong.B: "Tier 0 (Critical-Plus)" is not a defined tier.

questions.exam_reasoning: Distinguishes non-essential assets from essential and important tiers.

source_reference.syllabus_section: Domain 2 > Asset Security > Asset Classification Tiers

questions.question: Development environments and backup systems are classified under which asset tier?

explanation.why_correct: Tier 1 (Important) includes development environments and backup systems.

why_others_are_wrong.A: Tier 0 is essential infrastructure (critical servers, databases, network devices).
why_others_are_wrong.C: Tier 2 is non-essential (workstations, mobile devices, printers).
why_others_are_wrong.B: Unclassified is a data classification level, not an asset tier.

questions.exam_reasoning: Recall of the middle asset tier.

source_reference.syllabus_section: Domain 2 > Asset Security > Asset Classification Tiers

questions.question: Data that can uniquely identify an individual and is subject to strict regulatory standards is known as:

explanation.why_correct: PII is data that can uniquely identify an individual and is subject to strict regulatory standards.

why_others_are_wrong.B: PHI is specifically health-related information protected under laws like HIPAA.
why_others_are_wrong.D: Proprietary data gives a business competitive advantage.
why_others_are_wrong.C: Public data has minimal sensitivity.

questions.exam_reasoning: Recall of the PII definition.

source_reference.syllabus_section: Domain 2 > Asset Security > Types of Sensitive Data

questions.question: Health-related information that requires protection under laws such as HIPAA is categorized as:

explanation.why_correct: PHI is health-related information requiring protection under laws like HIPAA.

why_others_are_wrong.C: PII identifies individuals generally but is not specifically health data.
why_others_are_wrong.D: Proprietary data provides competitive advantage, unrelated to health.
why_others_are_wrong.B: Tier 0 is an asset tier, not a data type.

questions.exam_reasoning: Distinguishes PHI from PII and proprietary data.

source_reference.syllabus_section: Domain 2 > Asset Security > Types of Sensitive Data

questions.question: Information that gives a business a competitive advantage and therefore requires high-level security is BEST described as:

explanation.why_correct: Proprietary data gives a business competitive advantage and requires high-level security.

why_others_are_wrong.D: Public data carries minimal sensitivity.
why_others_are_wrong.A: Unclassified data has low or no impact.
why_others_are_wrong.B: PII identifies individuals; it is not defined by competitive advantage.

questions.exam_reasoning: Maps competitive-advantage information to proprietary data.

source_reference.syllabus_section: Domain 2 > Asset Security > Types of Sensitive Data

questions.question: Which TWO of the following are categories of sensitive data that warrant heightened protection? (Select TWO.)

options.label: A
options.text: Press releases already distributed to the media

options.label: D
options.text: Public marketing brochures posted on the company website

explanation.why_correct: PII and PHI are sensitive data types subject to regulatory protection; public materials are not sensitive.

why_others_are_wrong.D: Public marketing brochures are intentionally public and not sensitive.
why_others_are_wrong.A: Distributed press releases are public information, not sensitive data.

questions.exam_reasoning: Separates regulated sensitive data from intentionally public information.

source_reference.syllabus_section: Domain 2 > Asset Security > Types of Sensitive Data

questions.question: Which NIST Special Publication is referenced as essential for understanding data types and classification standards?

explanation.why_correct: NIST SP 800-60 provides guidance on mapping information and information system types to security categories (data types and classification).

why_others_are_wrong.D: NIST SP 800-88 covers media sanitization.
why_others_are_wrong.B: NIST SP 800-37 is the Risk Management Framework.
why_others_are_wrong.C: NIST SP 1800-5 relates to IT asset management.

questions.exam_reasoning: Maps data-type/classification guidance to NIST SP 800-60.

source_reference.syllabus_section: Domain 2 > Asset Security > Important Reference

questions.question: A sensitivity assessment evaluates a data set's need for protection based primarily on its:

options.label: A
options.text: Number of backup copies that exist

options.label: B
options.text: The vendor that supplied the storage device

explanation.why_correct: Sensitivity assessment evaluates the data's need for protection based on its confidentiality, integrity, and availability.

why_others_are_wrong.C: Formatting does not determine protection requirements.
why_others_are_wrong.A: Backup count is a resilience detail, not a sensitivity measure.
why_others_are_wrong.B: Storage vendor is unrelated to data sensitivity.

questions.exam_reasoning: Ties sensitivity assessment to CIA-based protection needs.

source_reference.syllabus_section: Domain 2 > Asset Security > Data Classification

questions.question: Why is maintaining a comprehensive inventory of all data and assets important to classification?

options.label: B
options.text: It guarantees data can never be breached

options.label: C
options.text: It helps assess each item's criticality and impact on business operations

options.label: D
options.text: It removes the need to classify data at all

explanation.why_correct: A comprehensive inventory helps assess the criticality and business impact of data and assets, which underpins classification and protection.

why_others_are_wrong.B: An inventory supports protection but does not guarantee breach immunity.
why_others_are_wrong.D: Inventory enables classification; it does not replace it.
why_others_are_wrong.A: Inventory is a listing activity; it does not perform encryption.

questions.exam_reasoning: Connects asset inventory to criticality/impact assessment.

source_reference.syllabus_section: Domain 2 > Asset Security > Data Classification

questions.question: When identifying data types for classification, an organization should account for data in:

options.label: A
options.text: Neither format, because classification applies only to hardware

options.label: B
options.text: Digital formats only, since paper is never sensitive

options.label: D
options.text: Physical formats only, since digital data is automatically secure

explanation.why_correct: Data classification must consider both physical and digital formats of information.

why_others_are_wrong.B: Paper records can be highly sensitive and must be classified.
why_others_are_wrong.D: Digital data is not automatically secure and must be classified.
why_others_are_wrong.A: Classification applies to data/information, including but not limited to hardware.

questions.exam_reasoning: Reinforces that classification covers physical and digital data.

source_reference.syllabus_section: Domain 2 > Asset Security > Data Classification

questions.question: Which TWO are stated benefits of properly classifying assets? (Select TWO.)

options.label: B
options.text: Guaranteed elimination of all cyber risk

explanation.why_correct: Benefits of proper classification include improved security awareness, compliance assurance, and enhanced planning.

why_others_are_wrong.B: Classification reduces and manages risk but cannot eliminate it entirely.
why_others_are_wrong.C: Classification supports compliance; it does not exempt an organization from audits.

questions.exam_reasoning: Recall of classification benefits.

source_reference.syllabus_section: Domain 2 > Asset Security > Asset Classification Tiers

questions.question: During asset classification, a team maps exactly how sensitive data moves into, within, and out of the organization. The PRIMARY security value of tracking this data flow is to:

options.label: A
options.text: Increase the volume of data the organization stores

options.label: B
options.text: Replace the need to classify the data itself

options.label: C
options.text: Guarantee the data never needs encryption

options.label: D
options.text: Ensure appropriate security measures are applied wherever the data travels, including in transit

explanation.why_correct: Tracking the flow of data ensures appropriate controls are applied as data moves within and outside the organization, protecting it in all states including transit.

why_others_are_wrong.A: Mapping flow does not increase stored volume.
why_others_are_wrong.B: Flow analysis complements—not replaces—classification.
why_others_are_wrong.C: Data in transit often specifically requires encryption.

questions.exam_reasoning: Connects data-flow mapping to applying controls across data states.

source_reference.syllabus_section: Domain 2 > Asset Security > Asset Classification

questions.question: Policies governing data creation, collection, management, and disposal primarily help ensure:

options.label: A
options.text: Data quality, authenticity, and reliability, and regulatory compliance

options.label: B
options.text: That all data is deleted immediately upon creation

explanation.why_correct: Governance, regulation, and compliance policies over the data lifecycle help ensure data quality, authenticity, and reliability while meeting regulations.

why_others_are_wrong.C: Such governance supports classification rather than preventing it.
why_others_are_wrong.B: Immediate deletion would destroy needed data and ignore retention requirements.
why_others_are_wrong.D: Governance reinforces—not removes—the need for controls.

questions.exam_reasoning: Links data governance policies to quality and compliance outcomes.

source_reference.syllabus_section: Domain 2 > Asset Security > Data Classification

questions.question: A single system stores both public data and highly sensitive PII together (co-mingled). According to the high-watermark principle, the system should be protected at the level of:

options.label: A
options.text: The average sensitivity of all data on the system

options.label: B
options.text: The most sensitive data it contains (the PII)

options.label: C
options.text: Whatever level is cheapest to implement

options.label: D
options.text: The least sensitive data it contains (the public data)

explanation.why_correct: The high-watermark principle applies the highest level of protection required by the most sensitive data type present on a system.

why_others_are_wrong.D: Protecting to the lowest level would leave the sensitive PII exposed.
why_others_are_wrong.A: Averaging sensitivity under-protects the most sensitive data.
why_others_are_wrong.C: Cost cannot override the protection needs of the most sensitive data.

questions.exam_reasoning: Tests the high-watermark concept for co-mingled data.

source_reference.syllabus_section: Domain 2 > Data Security Controls > Control Baseline and Tailoring

questions.question: Which of the following is an example of "regulated information" that must be handled according to legal requirements?

options.label: C
options.text: Cardholder data subject to PCI DSS

explanation.why_correct: Regulated information includes data governed by laws/standards such as cardholder data under PCI DSS, which mandates specific handling.

why_others_are_wrong.A: A blank template contains no sensitive or regulated content.
why_others_are_wrong.D: A lunch menu is non-sensitive public information.
why_others_are_wrong.B: A public blog post is intentionally public, not regulated sensitive data.

questions.exam_reasoning: Identifies regulated data via a concrete PCI DSS example.

source_reference.syllabus_section: Domain 2 > Asset Security > Types of Sensitive Data

questions.question: Aligning a classification scheme with business needs primarily helps to:

options.label: A
options.text: Avoid documenting any data at all

options.label: B
options.text: Force every asset into the Top Secret level

options.label: C
options.text: Guarantee the organization never needs encryption

options.label: D
options.text: Minimize risk while strengthening security in a way that supports operations

explanation.why_correct: Aligning classification with business needs minimizes risks and strengthens security while supporting business operations.

why_others_are_wrong.B: Over-classifying all assets as Top Secret wastes resources and is not business-aligned.
why_others_are_wrong.A: Classification requires documenting/inventorying data, not avoiding it.
why_others_are_wrong.C: Alignment does not eliminate the need for controls such as encryption.

questions.exam_reasoning: Connects business-aligned classification to balanced risk reduction.

source_reference.syllabus_section: Domain 2 > Asset Security > Classifying Data and Assets

questions.question: Which TWO of the following are government data classification levels described in the guide? (Select TWO.)

explanation.why_correct: Top Secret and Confidential are government classification levels (along with Secret and Unclassified).

why_others_are_wrong.C: Tier 0 (Essential) is an asset tier, not a data classification level.
why_others_are_wrong.A: Proprietary describes a sensitive data type, not a government classification level.

questions.exam_reasoning: Separates government classification levels from asset tiers and data types.

source_reference.syllabus_section: Domain 2 > Asset Security > Classification Levels

questions.question: Which data role holds ultimate responsibility for a data set and typically delegates protection tasks to a custodian?

explanation.why_correct: The data owner is responsible for the data (often specialized by type, e.g., financial or medical) and delegates implementation to data custodians.

why_others_are_wrong.B: The custodian implements controls on the owner's behalf.
why_others_are_wrong.D: The steward is a subject-matter expert who assists with classification.
why_others_are_wrong.C: The data subject is the individual the data is about / who uses it.

questions.exam_reasoning: Recall of the owner's accountability and delegation to the custodian.

source_reference.syllabus_section: Domain 2 > Asset Security > Data Roles and Responsibilities

questions.question: Who implements the physical, administrative, and logical controls that protect data, working on behalf of the data owner?

explanation.why_correct: The data custodian implements physical, administrative, and logical controls on behalf of the owner and manages the technical protection of data.

why_others_are_wrong.B: The owner sets requirements and delegates; it does not necessarily implement controls.
why_others_are_wrong.D: The steward provides subject-matter expertise and assists with classification.
why_others_are_wrong.C: The processor (GDPR) acts on the controller's behalf to process data, a distinct role.

questions.exam_reasoning: Distinguishes the custodian's implementation role from the owner and steward.

source_reference.syllabus_section: Domain 2 > Asset Security > Data Roles and Responsibilities

questions.question: Which role acts as a subject-matter expert for specific data types and assists in classifying and categorizing the data?

explanation.why_correct: The data steward is a subject-matter expert for specific data types who assists with classification and works with both owner and custodian.

why_others_are_wrong.D: The custodian implements technical protection, not SME classification guidance.
why_others_are_wrong.B: The data subject is the individual whose data is processed or a system user.
why_others_are_wrong.A: Senior management is accountable for overall asset management, not data SME work.

questions.exam_reasoning: Maps SME classification assistance to the steward.

source_reference.syllabus_section: Domain 2 > Asset Security > Data Roles and Responsibilities

questions.question: In the guide's role model, "data subjects" include which of the following?

options.label: A
options.text: Human users and non-human entities (applications, scripts) that consume or interact with data

options.label: C
